title: Play-Doh began as wallpaper cleaner
hook: Before children squashed it into shapes, Play-Doh wiped soot off walls.
peek: In the 1930s a Cincinnati soap company sold a soft putty for rolling soot off wallpaper. When homes stopped burning coal, sales collapsed. Then a nursery school teacher let her pupils model with it, and the putty was reborn as one of the best-loved toys in the world.
lede: Homes heated with coal had grimy walls, and wallpaper could not be washed. In the 1930s Kutol Products of Cincinnati sold a soft, non-sticky putty that people rolled over the paper to lift the soot. After the Second World War, cleaner heating and washable vinyl wallpaper made it nearly useless, and the company was in trouble.

bullets.text: Kay Zufall, a nursery school teacher whose brother-in-law Joe McVicker worked at Kutol, read that the cleaner could be used for modelling. She tried it with her pupils, they loved it, and she urged the family to sell it as a toy.

The McVickers planned to call it Rainbow Modeling Compound. Zufall and her husband suggested Play-Doh instead. The putty went on sale as a toy in the mid-1950s, first only in off-white, with red, yellow and blue following soon after.
Play-Doh is mostly water, salt and flour, which is why it feels like dough and dries out if the lid is left off. The exact recipe is a trade secret.

In 2018 its owner Hasbro registered the scent as a trademark, describing it as a sweet, slightly musky vanilla with hints of cherry and salted, wheat-based dough. Few toys have a smell so recognisable that it needs legal protection.
